extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing inventive step (obviousness) and unity of invention for ARIPO patent applications, including definitions of the skilled person, problem-and-solution approach, secondary indicators, combining prior art, selection inventions, and allowable claim combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art (Section 3(10)(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'state of the art' concerns such kind of information as is relevant to some field of technology; it may reside in the relevant common general knowledge, which need not necessarily be in writing and needs substantiation only if challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all information relevant to the technical field, including unwritten common general knowledge. The state of the art includes documents cited in the search report and other material that would be available to the skilled person up to and including the day before filing/priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (Section 3(10)(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilled practitioner in the relevant field, possessed of average knowledge and ability, aware of common general knowledge at the relevant date, with access to the state of the art and normal means for routine work and experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be construed as an individual or a group (e.g. research/production team). The skilled person may look to neighbouring or remote fields if prompted. Use this specialist's knowledge and ability as the baseline for assessing inventive step and sufficiency of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (general test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether, before the filing or priority date, having regard to the art known at the time, it would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something falling within the terms of the claim; if so, the claim lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Obvious’ means following plainly or logically from prior art without exercise of skill beyond that expected of the skilled person. Construed in light of knowledge up to and including the day before filing/priority. Distinguish inventive step from novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess inventive step objectively and predictably, apply the problem-and-solution approach (deviation should be exceptional). The approach has three stages: (i) determine the closest prior art, (ii) establish the objective technical problem, (iii) consider whether the claimed invention would have been obvious starting from the closest prior art and the objective problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the three-stage method to avoid ex post facto reasoning and to structure the inventive-step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is a single reference disclosing the combination of features that constitutes the most promising starting point for an obvious development leading to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer references directed to a similar purpose/effect or belonging to same/closely related technical field; choose the reference requiring minimum structural/functional modifications to reach the claimed invention. Assess from the skilled person's point of view on the day before filing. Consider applicant's own acknowledgements in the description/claims as correct unless contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation of the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the application/patent, the closest prior art, and the distinguishing feature(s); identify the technical effect of the distinguishing features and formulate the technical problem (the aim/task of adapting the closest prior art to provide those technical effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignore features that do not contribute to technical character. The objective technical problem may require reformulation relative to the applicant's stated problem based on objectively established facts (e.g., search report prior art). Reformulation may use any effect derivable from the application as filed; new effects submitted later are allowable only if the skilled person would recognize them as implied by or related to the originally suggested technical problem. Do not formulate the problem so as to contain pointers to the technical solution (avoid ex post facto framing). The technical problem can be broad (e.g., seeking an alternative) and may be an aggregation of partial problems when different distinguishing features solve different partial problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could–would approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In the third stage ask whether there is any teaching in the prior art that would (not simply could) have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art and thereby arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a motivation or incentive in the prior art that would have led the skilled person to combine or modify disclosures; implicit prompting is sufficient. The motivating teaching must have been present before the filing/priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining pieces of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible to combine disclosure of one or more documents, parts of documents, or other prior-art pieces with the closest prior art, but the need to combine many disclosures may indicate an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether it is permissible to combine, consider compatibility of disclosures (inherent incompatibility argues against combination), whether disclosures come from similar/neighboring/remote fields, and whether there is a reasonable basis for associating parts (e.g., textbooks, standards, or explicit cross-references). Different documents may be combined for different partial problems in a multi-problem invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs. juxtaposition or aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be considered as a whole. If a claim is an aggregation/juxtaposition of features without functional interaction it may be obvious even though individual features are known; a combination of features requires functional interaction producing a synergistic technical effect different from the sum of individual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for synergistic interaction (example: transistors forming a microprocessor produce data-processing effects beyond individual transistor switching). If no synergistic effect exists, treating the claim as a mere aggregation may defeat inventive-step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post facto analysis caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of reconstructive reasoning that shows theoretically how an idea could have been arrived at from known matter by a series of apparently easy steps; such hindsight can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize the overall state of the art confronting the skilled person before the applicant's contribution. Recognize that search report documents were found with foreknowledge of the alleged invention. Give fair weight to arguments/evidence from the applicant and be hesitant to sustain inventive-step objections when a convincing technical advantage is shown and plausibly linked to claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of an invention (possible bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be based on devising a solution to a known problem, arriving at an insight into the cause of an observed phenomenon (with the practical use then being obvious), or combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (e.g., freeze-branding of cattle; identifying a flavour-causing compound and applying it as a margarine additive) to illustrate that arriving at insight plus its application can involve inventive faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicators — predictable disadvantage / non-functional modification / arbitrary choice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention results from a foreseeable disadvantageous modification of the closest prior art, clearly predictable and not accompanied by unexpected technical advantage, then it lacks inventive step. Similarly for arbitrary non-functional modifications or arbitrary selection from many solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere foreseeable worsening without unexpected advantage is not inventive. If the worsening is accompanied by an unexpected technical advantage, inventive step might exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicators — unexpected technical effect; bonus effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An unexpected technical effect may indicate inventive step. However, if the skilled person would have arrived at the subject-matter anyway (e.g., a one-way-street situation with no alternatives), the unexpected effect may be a mere bonus that does not confer inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the unexpected effect is genuinely surprising and whether it changes the obviousness conclusion, bearing in mind the prior-art context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicators — long-felt need; commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving a long-standing technical problem or fulfilling a long-felt need may indicate inventive step. Commercial success alone is not indicative unless coupled with evidence that success derives from technical features of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require examiner satisfaction that commercial success is due to the invention's technical merits rather than external factors (marketing, selling techniques). Immediate commercial success with evidence of long-felt want is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments and evidence submitted by the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments and evidence may come from the originally filed application or be submitted during proceedings; new effects can be taken into account only if they are implied by or related to the technical problem initially suggested in the originally filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully assess new effects. Example: a pharmaceutical composition originally filed for activity may later be supported by evidence of unexpected low toxicity; this is allowable to reformulate the problem if activity and toxicity are related and the skilled person would consider them together. Reformulation may lead to amendments of the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection inventions represent selected sub-sets or sub-ranges of known ranges. If the selection is connected to a particular technical effect and no hints exist leading the skilled person to make that selection, an inventive step is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the skilled person would have made the selection 'in the hope of solving the underlying technical problem or in expectation of some improvement'. Distinguish from the novelty test for overlapping ranges (the 'seriously contemplating' test). An unexpected degree of effect within the selected range can support inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims and claims in different categories
rubrics_metrics.description: If an independent claim is new and non-obvious, generally there is no need to investigate novelty/non-obviousness of dependent claims, except where dependent claims have a later effective date requiring consideration of intermediate documents. Similarly, if a product claim is new and non-obvious there is no need to examine a process claim which inevitably results in the manufacture of that product, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that analogy processes that lack inventive step may still be patentable insofar as they provide a novel and inventive product. Where product, process and use claims have different effective dates, separate examination may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of known measures — obvious cases (3.7.17.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions involving application of known measures in an obvious way are non-inventive; examples include filling an incomplete teaching by the naturally occurring choice, mere use of well-known equivalents, new use of a known material using its known properties, analogous substitution of a newly developed but plainly suitable material, or use of a known technique in a closely analogous situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) prior document omits explicit mention of aluminium though same structure disclosed; (ii) substituting hydraulic for electric motor; (iii) known detergent compound used as detergent because of known property; (iv) using a newly developed adhesive plainly suitable for polymer-metal bonding; (v) applying a known pulse control technique analogously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of known measures — non-obvious cases (3.7.17.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A known method or means used for a different purpose that involves a new, surprising effect or a new use that requires overcoming technical difficulties not resolvable by routine techniques can be inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: high-frequency power used in a new welding context producing unexpected effect (scale removal unnecessary); adapting a device known in one application to another where new practical difficulties must be overcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious combination of features (3.7.17.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition or association of known devices/processes functioning in their normal way and not producing any non-obvious inter-relationship is obvious and non-inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: placing a known mincing machine and a known filling machine side by side to make a sausage-producing machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not-obvious (inventive) combination of features (3.7.17.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combined features that mutually support each other in their effects to such an extent that a new technical result is achieved are not obvious, even if individual features are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevant whether individual features are known. Beware of 'bonus effect' combinations resulting from one-way-street situations which may still lack inventiveness. Example: combining an analgesic with a sedative produces an intensified analgesic effect unpredictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious selection among known possibilities (3.7.17.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection is obvious where invention consists merely in choosing from equally likely alternatives, selecting parameters from a limited range derivable by routine trial and error, simple extrapolation from known art, or selecting particular compounds from a broad field when no unexpected advantage is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include choosing one well-known alternative heating method, selecting routine flow rates, straight-line extrapolation on graphs, or selecting substituents from broadly defined R groups that give no unexpected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not-obvious selection among known possibilities (3.7.17.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection is inventive where particular operating conditions or compounds selected from a broad field produce unexpected effects and there are no indications leading the skilled person to make that selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discovering a narrow temperature window (63–65 °C) with unexpectedly higher yield; selecting particular substituents that yield unanticipated advantageous properties absent any pointer in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a technical prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art leads the skilled person away from carrying out the procedure proposed by the invention, an inventive step generally exists, particularly when the skilled person would not have considered attempting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a bottling process that omits conventionally necessary air-shielding steps yet works demonstrates inventive step because prior opinion discouraged trying such an approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention (Section 2(9)(a), Rule 7(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: An ARIPO application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept; the link must be a technical relationship expressed by the same or corresponding special technical features in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special technical features are those defining the contribution over the prior art. Correspondence (e.g., different means achieving the same functional effect) suffices. A single general inventive concept may permit multiple independent claims in different categories (product/process/use); specified combinations (i)-(iii) are generally permissible, but multiple such sets are allowed only exceptionally and require the single-concept link to be present. Phrases like 'specially adapted' do not by themselves establish a single general inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combinations of claim categories (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: ARIPO permits inclusion, as part of a single-concept linked group, combinations such as: (i) an independent product claim plus an independent process claim specially adapted to manufacture that product and an independent use claim for that product; (ii) a process claim and an apparatus or means specifically designed for carrying out the process; (iii) product + specially adapted manufacturing process + apparatus for the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process is 'specially adapted' for manufacture of a product if it results in the claimed product and thus defines a technical relationship. A manufacturing process and its product do not lack unity merely because the process is not limited to making that product. Multiple sets of such combinations in one application are exceptional.
